Monastic
mō-năs´tĭk
adj. (pertaining to monks or to the life of religious seclusion under vows)
Greek monazein, to live alone, from monos, alone. Luther and Calvin were both formed by the system before they wrote against it; Luther had taken the vows.

Biblical Definition

The monastic life withdraws from ordinary society under vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. The Lord prays the opposite for His own: “I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil” (John 17:15). Paul says separation from sinners is impossible anyway, “for then must ye needs go out of the world” (1Co 5:10). He names compulsory celibacy and abstinence as doctrines of devils, “forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3), and says such severity is “not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23). The commission runs outward: “a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines monastic as pertaining to monasteries, monks and nuns; recluse; secluded from the temporal concerns of life and devoted to religion.

expand to see more

MONASTIC, MONASTICAL, a. Pertaining to monasteries, monks and nuns; as monastic life; monastic vows.

2. Recluse; secluded from the temporal concerns of life, and devoted to religion.

MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from ordinary temporal concerns, whether an abbey, a priory or a convent.

Key Scripture

John 17:15 — "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil."

1Co 5:10 — "Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world."

1Ti 4:3 — "Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth."

Col 2:23 — "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh."

Mat 5:14 — "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid."

Modern Corruption

A two-tier Christianity is created in which the vowed are the serious ones, and the New Testament knows only one tier.

expand to see more

The deepest objection is not to the discipline but to the ranking. Monasticism institutionalised the idea that there are counsels of perfection above the commands binding on all — that a man may be an ordinary Christian by keeping the commandments and a superior one by adding poverty, celibacy and obedience. Once that is granted, the mother, the farmer and the magistrate are second-class by definition, and the Reformation's doctrine of vocation was the answer: a milkmaid milking to the glory of God is doing holy work, and there is no higher category to aspire to.

First Timothy 4:3 uses language no one would choose lightly. Forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats is called a doctrine of devils, not an excess of zeal — because it implicates the doctrine of creation, denying that God made these things to be received with thanksgiving. Colossians 2:23 adds the practical verdict, and it is the one that would most have surprised the monasteries: the severity has a shew of wisdom and is not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh. It does not achieve what it exists to achieve. A man does not leave his sin at the gate; he takes it in with him, and the cell will teach him that.

Justice requires the other half. The monasteries copied the Scriptures through centuries when nobody else would, kept learning alive, fed the poor, and produced Bernard and Anselm, whom Calvin cites with respect. And the impulse behind them — that following Christ should cost something visible — is sound, and rebukes a comfortable Protestantism that has often let discipleship cost nothing at all. The answer to a wrong location for that seriousness is not to abolish the seriousness. John 17:15 gives its right shape: kept in the world, kept from the evil, and sent into it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kosmos (G2889), world; tereo (G5083), to keep, guard; apechomai (G567), to abstain; ethelothreskeia (G1479), will worship.

expand to see more

Greek ek tou kosmou (G2889) — out of the world; John 17:15–18, 1 Corinthians 5:10.

Greek tereo ek (G5083) — to keep from; John 17:15, Revelation 3:10.

Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — will worship, self-chosen devotion; Colossians 2:23 only.

Usage

"“Not that thou shouldest take them out of the world” — the prayer He actually prayed."

"“Then must ye needs go out of the world” — Paul, on total separation."

"“Not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” — the severity does not work."
